config.title: Reusable Button

intro.title: Reusable Button
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a reusable Button component in React with TypeScript. You will learn how to create a single, flexible component that can be used throughout an application with different labels, styles, and behaviors. The core concept is using React props to make components dynamic and configurable. You will work with TypeScript interfaces to define the component's expected properties, ensuring type safety. By the end, you'll have a customizable button that can handle clicks and display various text.
intro.usecase: Reusable buttons are fundamental building blocks in modern web applications, appearing everywhere from e-commerce checkout flows to social media interfaces. In a dashboard application, you might use them for actions like 'Save Report', 'Export Data', or 'Filter Results' with consistent styling and behavior. Form submissions, modal confirmations, and navigation menus all rely on reusable button components to maintain visual consistency and reduce code duplication. As a developer, creating a well-designed reusable button component saves time and ensures a cohesive user experience across your entire application.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define a reusable button component's props structure
Implement a functional React component with typed props to create a reusable button
Utilize destructuring assignment to extract specific props within the component function
Apply conditional logic to control button styling based on variant props
Construct JSX elements with dynamic className attributes using template literals
Execute event handling by passing onClick callbacks through component props
Use TypeScript generics to define children props for flexible button content
Implement default prop values to ensure consistent button behavior
Apply React's forwardRef pattern to expose DOM element references
Construct and export the button component for reuse across the application

steps.title: Import React from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React from the 'react' package to enable React component creation.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React into your file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React
import React from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library is imported, allowing you to use React components and JSX.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React. This is the foundation for creating React components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement might be incomplete. Make sure you're importing React from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the Button component function
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Button that returns null for now. Use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component function that takes no props and returns null. This is a placeholder that we'll fill with actual JSX later.
steps.seedCode:
import React from 'react';

// Create the Button component function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Button component function is defined that returns null.
successCriteria: Component is a valid TypeScript function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Button component function. This is the foundation we'll build upon.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'Button'? Does it return null? Is it a valid TypeScript function?
steps.feedbackWrong: The Button component wasn't created correctly. Make sure you define a function named Button that returns null.

steps.title: Define the ButtonProps interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'ButtonProps' with two properties: 'label' (type string) and 'onClick' (type () => void). Place this interface above the Button component function.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions. Remember to include the correct types for both properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a ButtonProps interface defined with the correct property types, ready to be used as the props type for your Button component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the ButtonProps interface with the correct property types. This will provide type safety for your reusable button component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface includes both required properties with the correct TypeScript types: 'label' should be string and 'onClick' should be () => void.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ButtonProps interface wasn't defined correctly. Make sure you use the 'interface' keyword, name it 'ButtonProps', and include both 'label: string' and 'onClick: () => void' properties.

steps.title: Add ButtonProps to the component
steps.instruction: Add the ButtonProps interface as the type for the Button component's props parameter. The component should accept a single props parameter typed with ButtonProps.
steps.hint: In TypeScript React components, you type the props parameter directly in the function signature. For example: `function MyComponent(props: MyProps) { ... }`
steps.expectedOutcome: The Button component now has a typed props parameter using the ButtonProps interface, making it ready to receive props.
successCriteria: props parameter is typed with ButtonProps interface
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the ButtonProps type to your component's props parameter. This ensures TypeScript will validate that the component receives the correct props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the props parameter to the Button function and typed it with the ButtonProps interface. Check that your function signature looks like `function Button(props: ButtonProps)`.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Button component doesn't have a properly typed props parameter. Remember to add `props: ButtonProps` as the parameter to the Button function.

steps.title: Destructure props in the component
steps.instruction: Inside the Button component, destructure the label property from the props parameter.
steps.hint: Use object destructuring syntax in the function parameters to extract the label property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Button component should now have a destructured label parameter, making it accessible inside the function body.
successCriteria: The Button function signature includes destructured props
The label property is extracted from props using object destructuring
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully destructured the label prop from the ButtonProps interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're destructuring the label property directly in the function parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to destructure the label property from the props parameter in the Button function signature.

steps.title: Return a button element with the label
steps.instruction: Inside the Button component, return a button element that displays the label prop as its content.
steps.hint: Use JSX to return a <button> element with the label variable inside it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Button component will render a button displaying the label passed as a prop.
successCriteria: Button element uses the label prop as content
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully made the button display the dynamic label from props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the button's content is the label prop, not static text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button should display the label prop. Check that you're using the label variable inside the button element.

steps.title: Wire the onClick handler to the button
steps.instruction: Add the onClick prop to the button element and pass the onClick handler from props.
steps.hint: In the button element, add an onClick attribute and set it equal to the onClick prop you destructured earlier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring an onClick handler to a button
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button element will have an onClick prop that calls the onClick function passed from the parent component when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element includes an onClick attribute
The onClick attribute is set to the onClick prop from ButtonProps
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the onClick handler to the button element. Now the button will respond to clicks by calling the function passed from the parent component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the onClick prop from the ButtonProps interface. The button element should have an onClick attribute that references the onClick prop you destructured.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on adding the onClick prop to the button. Remember to add the onClick attribute to the button element and set it equal to the onClick prop from your ButtonProps.

steps.title: Export the Button component
steps.instruction: Export the Button component as the default export so it can be imported in other files.
steps.hint: Use the 'export default' syntax followed by the component name.
steps.analogousExample:
// Export a component as default
export default Button;
steps.expectedOutcome: The Button component is exported as the default export, making it available for import in other files.
successCriteria: The code should include 'export default Button;' (or equivalent) after the Button component definition.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the Button component as the default export. This makes it available for import in other files.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the correct export syntax. Try using 'export default Button;' after the component definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Button component isn't properly exported. Add 'export default Button;' after the component definition to make it available for import.

steps.title: Create a test App component
steps.instruction: Create a new function component called App that will use the Button component. The App component should return a JSX structure.
steps.hint: Define a function named App that returns some JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a new App component function that can serve as a parent component to test the Button component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component. This will serve as the parent component where we can test our reusable Button.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a component named 'App' that returns JSX. Check that you used the correct name and included a return statement with JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component wasn't created correctly. Make sure to define a function or arrow function named 'App' that returns JSX.

steps.title: Use the Button component in App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the Button component with label and onClick props.
steps.hint: Render the Button component like any other JSX element, passing the required props.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component renders a Button with a label and click handler.
successCriteria: Button component is rendered inside App
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used the reusable Button component with its required props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're rendering the Button component with both label and onClick props.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using the Button component inside App with the required props.
